title: Where Am I? (CD)
brief: The laptop is already open at a Command Prompt. In Windows CMD, running `cd` with no arguments prints the directory you are in — run it and see whose profile you have landed in.
objective: Print the directory you are standing in.

hints.text: Type `cd` and press Enter.

successMessage: The profile folder is your first clue about the owner. `chdir` is the same command under a longer name.

title: Directory Listing (DIR)
brief: Run `dir` to list the files and folders of the profile you have landed in.
objective: List the files and folders of the profile you have landed in.

hints.text: Type `dir`.

successMessage: `dir` shows dates, sizes and a `<DIR>` marker for folders. Five folders here — and, as you will find out, not everything is on this list.

title: Show All Files (DIR /A)
brief: One file in this folder never turns up in a plain `dir`: Windows hides a file with an attribute letter (H for Hidden) rather than with a leading dot. Make `dir` show everything, hidden files included.
objective: List everything in this folder, hidden files included.

hints.text: `dir` switches start with a forward slash. The one for attributes is `/a`.
Run `dir /a`.

successMessage: `lostfound.tag` was there the whole time. `/a` includes files with any attribute set, hidden ones among them.

title: Bare Listing (DIR /B)
brief: Produce a clean listing of this folder: names only, with no header, no sizes and no summary line. Use `dir`.
objective: List this folder as names only — no header, no sizes, no summary line.

hints.text: The `dir` switch for a bare listing is `/b`.
Run `dir /b`.

successMessage: Bare output is what you pipe into another command. Headers and totals only get in the way there.

title: Recursive Search (DIR /S)
brief: List `Documents` AND every folder inside it in one go. Use `dir`.
objective: List `Documents` and every folder inside it in one command.

hints.text: The `dir` switch that walks down into subfolders is `/s`.
Run `dir /s Documents`.

successMessage: `/s` is how you search a machine you do not know. It is also how you accidentally print ten thousand lines, so aim it at a folder.

title: Enter Documents (CD)
brief: The owner's paperwork is in `Documents`. Run `cd Documents` to move into it.
objective: Move into the `Documents` folder.

hints.text: Type `cd Documents`.

successMessage: The prompt now shows `C:\Users\Student\Documents`. In CMD the prompt is your position indicator.

title: Climb to Parent (CD ..)
brief: Run `cd ..` from `Documents` to climb back up to the profile folder.
objective: Move from `Documents` back up to the profile folder.

hints.text: Type `cd ..`.

successMessage: `..` means the parent folder on Windows exactly as it does on Linux. The slashes differ; the idea does not.

title: Display File Content (TYPE)
brief: Print `Documents\notes.txt` to the prompt and find out what domain this laptop belongs to. Windows has no `cat`.
objective: Print `Documents\notes.txt` to the prompt.

success.text:
Project Status: Windows Rollout
Domain: CORP.INTERNAL
Administrator: Student

hints.text: The cmd.exe command that prints a file is `type`.
Run `type Documents\notes.txt`.

successMessage: CORP.INTERNAL, and an account called Student. Two more lines for the property form.

title: Directory Tree (TREE)
brief: Show this folder and everything under it as a picture of the hierarchy rather than a flat list.
objective: Show this folder and everything under it as a picture of the hierarchy.

hints.text: The command is `tree`. Adding `/f` lists the files as well as the folders.
Run `tree`.

successMessage: `tree /f` is the fastest way to see the shape of an unfamiliar machine — including the hidden tag.

title: Locate Binaries (WHERE)
brief: Find out where on this disk the command interpreter itself lives — the program `cmd`.
objective: Find where the program `cmd` lives on this disk.

hints.text: `where` searches the folders on PATH for a named program, the way `which` does on Linux.
Run `where cmd`.

successMessage: Knowing which copy of a program you are actually running is how you settle "but it works on my machine".

title: BOSS: The Four Servers
brief: Somewhere under this profile is a file listing four servers and one recovery code. Nobody will tell you where it is: walk the disk until you find it, print it, and submit the recovery code — it was generated for you alone.
objective: Find the file listing four servers, print it, and submit the recovery code inside.

hints.text: A recursive listing shows every file on the machine at once. Both `dir` and `tree` can do that with the right switch.
The file is `Documents\servers.txt`. Print it with `type`, then paste the FIND{...} value into the box.

successMessage: A domain controller, a file server, a database and a web server — and a recovery code that was yours alone. Search first, read second.

title: Copy Files (COPY)
brief: Never edit the only copy of anything. Make a duplicate of `Documents\notes.txt` called `Documents\notes_backup.txt`.
objective: Copy `Documents\notes.txt` to `Documents\notes_backup.txt`.

hints.text: One cmd.exe command duplicates a file without touching the original. It takes the existing file first, then the path for the copy.
Run `copy Documents\notes.txt Documents\notes_backup.txt`.

successMessage: Both files now exist and hold the same text. `copy` never touches the original.

title: Move Files (MOVE)
brief: The owner left a to-do list loose on the Desktop. Move `Desktop\todo.txt` into the `Documents` folder, keeping the same filename.
objective: Move `Desktop\todo.txt` into the `Documents` folder, keeping the same filename.

hints.text: A different command relocates a file instead of duplicating it — same two-argument order as before, but nothing survives at the old path afterward.
Run `move Desktop\todo.txt Documents\todo.txt`.

successMessage: Unlike `copy`, `move` leaves nothing behind at the source. The file exists once, in the new place.

title: Rename Files (REN)
brief: Rename `Desktop\Shortcut.lnk` to `AppShortcut.lnk`. It must stay on the Desktop.
objective: Rename `Desktop\Shortcut.lnk` to `AppShortcut.lnk`, leaving it on the Desktop.

hints.text: Renaming is a command of its own, separate from moving a file. Give it the existing path, then only the new name — a bare name, not a second full path, since the file is not going anywhere.
Run `ren Desktop\Shortcut.lnk AppShortcut.lnk`.

successMessage: A second path would be a `move`. `ren` only ever changes the name in place, which is why it takes a bare name.

title: Delete Files (DEL)
brief: `Downloads\archive.zip` is junk the owner will not want back. Delete it — and on the same line list `Downloads` again so you can see it has gone. In cmd.exe, `&` runs one command after another.
objective: Delete `Downloads\archive.zip` and, on the same line, list `Downloads` to see that it went.

hints.text: Deleting a file at the cmd.exe prompt takes one command and a path — no confirmation dialog, no Recycle Bin. Chain a listing after it with `&` so you watch the file actually disappear.
Run `del Downloads\archive.zip & dir /b Downloads`.

successMessage: One file left, and you watched it happen rather than assuming. A deletion from CMD does not go to the Recycle Bin.

title: Create Directories (MD / MKDIR)
brief: Create a folder called `Backup` in the profile folder, to hold what you are about to put aside.
objective: Create a folder called `Backup` in the profile folder.

hints.text: cmd.exe has a short spelling and a long spelling for the same command that creates a folder. Give it the name you want.
Run `md Backup`.

successMessage: Two names, one command. Old CMD habits kept the short forms alive.

title: Remove Directories (RD / RMDIR)
brief: The owner left an empty `Projects` folder behind and it is not going back with the laptop. Remove it, and on the same line list the profile folder again so you can see it has gone.
objective: Remove the empty `Projects` folder and, on the same line, list the profile folder to see that it went.

hints.text: The command that removes a folder also comes in a short and a long spelling, and refuses to run if anything is still inside. Chain a listing after it with `&` to see the folder gone.
Run `rd Projects & dir /b`.

successMessage: Four folders left. `rd` refuses a folder that still has anything in it, which is a safety feature, not an obstacle.

title: Inspect File Attributes (ATTRIB)
brief: `Documents\hidden_config.ini` does not appear in a plain `dir` either. Show which attribute letters are set on it.
objective: Show which attribute letters are set on `Documents\hidden_config.ini`.

hints.text: One command reports a file's attribute letters without changing anything — give it the path and read what comes back: H is Hidden, R is Read-only, S is System, A is Archive.
Run `attrib Documents\hidden_config.ini`.

successMessage: A and H. Hidden on Windows is one bit of metadata, not a security boundary — anyone who asks can see the file.

title: Environment Variables (%VAR%)
brief: cmd.exe wraps an environment variable in percent signs, like `%NAME%`. Print the value that `USERPROFILE` holds on this machine.
objective: Print the value that `USERPROFILE` holds on this machine.

hints.text: One command just prints whatever text it is given. cmd.exe swaps `%VAR%` for its value before that command ever runs, so it never even sees a variable name.
Run `echo %USERPROFILE%`.

successMessage: The shell replaced `%USERPROFILE%` with C:\Users\Student before echo ran. Echo itself never knew there was a variable.

title: Setting Variables (SET)
brief: You just read `%USERPROFILE%` back from the environment — now put something of your own into it. Every later write into `Documents` should trace back to this laptop's case, so set a marker before you copy anything else: `MY_VAR` holding `123`, printed back on the same line to prove it took. `set` prints nothing when it works, and `&` joins two commands.
objective: Set `MY_VAR` to `123`, then print it back on the same line to prove it took.

hints.text: One new command creates the variable with no spaces around the equals sign. `echo` prints it back the same way you just used, inside percent signs, joined on the same line with `&`.
Run `set MY_VAR=123 & echo %MY_VAR%`.

successMessage: MY_VAR now holds 123, and printing it back is what proved the assignment actually happened. That is the same check you will run the moment a marker that matters is riding on it.

title: Clear the Console (CLS)
brief: The screen is cluttered with everything you have run so far. Clear it.
objective: Clear the screen.

hints.text: cmd.exe has one command for wiping the screen, and it takes nothing after it — no path, no switch, just the word on its own.
Run `cls`.

successMessage: Clearing the screen does not clear anything else: your variables, your folder and your history all survive.

title: BOSS: Ready for Collection
brief: Put the paperwork together for the front desk. Make a folder called `Return`, copy `Documents\notes.txt` into it, and list that folder to prove the copy landed — all on one line, joined with `&`.
objective: In one line: make a `Return` folder, copy `Documents\notes.txt` into it, and list that folder to prove the copy landed.

hints.text: Three commands in a row on one line: make the directory, copy the file into it, then list what is inside it to prove it landed.
Run `md Return & copy Documents\notes.txt Return\notes.txt & dir /b Return`.

successMessage: Make, copy, verify. The listing at the end is the part that turns a hopeful command into a finished job.
solution: md Return & copy Documents\notes.txt Return\notes.txt & dir /b Return
acceptedVariants: md Return & copy Documents\notes.txt Return\notes.txt & dir /b Return
mkdir Return & copy Documents\notes.txt Return\notes.txt & dir /b Return

title: Pattern Search (FINDSTR)
brief: The property form asks what this machine was doing. Show every line in `logs\eventlog.txt` about a new process being created. Windows has no `grep`.
objective: Show every line in `logs\eventlog.txt` about a new process being created.

hints.text: cmd.exe's tool for searching inside a file takes the phrase to look for first, then the file to search — quote the phrase, since this one has spaces in it.
Run `findstr "A new process" logs\eventlog.txt`.

successMessage: Two processes: a hashing tool and a directory listing. Somebody was already poking around this machine.

title: Case-Insensitive FINDSTR (/I)
brief: The form asks whether the machine's protection was switched on. The event log names the product inconsistently — sometimes capitalised, sometimes not — so a search that matches one spelling misses the rest.
objective: Find every mention of `defender` in `logs\eventlog.txt`, whatever its capitalisation.

predicates.text: [EVENT ID 7036] The Windows Defender Antivirus Service entered the running state.

hints.text: `findstr` switches start with a forward slash. The one that ignores case is `/i`.
Run `findstr /i defender logs\eventlog.txt`.

successMessage: The log says Defender with a capital D. Without `/i` a search for `defender` finds nothing at all — content search is case-sensitive by default. Paths and filenames are the opposite: `documents` and `Documents` name the same folder.

title: Count Lines (FIND /C /V "")
brief: Count how many lines `logs\firewall.log` contains. cmd.exe has no `wc`, so the standard trick is to print the file and pipe it into a counter that counts every line NOT matching an empty pattern.
objective: Count how many lines `logs\firewall.log` contains.

hints.text: cmd.exe's line-counting trick reuses a search tool: point it at a pattern so broad that every single line matches, and ask it to report a count of matches instead of the matching text.
Run `type logs\firewall.log | find /c /v ""`.

successMessage: Five lines, one of them the header. This double negative is genuinely the standard Windows way to count lines.

title: Process List (TASKLIST)
brief: Record what is running on the machine before you shut it down. Show every process, with its memory use.
objective: Show every process running on the machine, with its memory use.

hints.text: cmd.exe's equivalent of Task Manager takes nothing after it — no path, no switch, just the command on its own — and lists every running process with its memory use.
Run `tasklist`.

successMessage: Same information as Task Manager, in a form you can pipe into something else.

title: Network Configuration (IPCONFIG)
brief: The form has a line for the network the laptop was last on. Show this machine's IPv4 address and adapter configuration.
objective: Show this machine's IPv4 address and adapter configuration.

hints.text: One cmd.exe command, run with nothing after it, reports every network adapter on this machine and the address each one holds.
Run `ipconfig`.

successMessage: 192.168.1.105, on the same 192.168.1.x network as the four servers you found in Act I.

title: System Information (SYSTEMINFO)
brief: The form wants the operating system build and the installed memory. Display the machine's system summary.
objective: Display the machine's system summary, with the operating system build and the installed memory.

hints.text: One cmd.exe command, run with nothing after it, dumps the machine's whole system summary — OS build, installed memory, all of it.
Run `systeminfo`.

successMessage: Windows 10 Pro, build 19045, 16 GB. Three more boxes on the form filled in from one command.

title: Cryptographic Hash (CERTUTIL)
brief: The form wants a checksum of `Documents\data.csv`, so that nobody can alter it between now and collection without it showing. Compute its MD5. Windows has no `md5sum`; the built-in tool is `certutil`.
objective: Compute the MD5 checksum of `Documents\data.csv`.

hints.text: One cmd.exe tool computes a file's hash. It needs a switch that names the file to hash, then the path, then the algorithm name in capitals.
Run `certutil -hashfile Documents\data.csv MD5`.

successMessage: Change one byte of that file and the hash changes completely. That is what makes it a receipt.

title: BOSS: Name on the Ticket
brief: The last line of the form is the one that matters: which account logged on to this machine successfully. Windows records that as event 4624 in `logs\eventlog.txt`. Print exactly that one line, and nothing else.
objective: Print the one line in `logs\eventlog.txt` that records a successful logon, and nothing else.

success.text: [EVENT ID 4624] An account was successfully logged on: TargetUserName: Student

hints.text: Two ways in, and both work: search the log for the event number, or search it for the words that describe a successful logon.
Run `findstr 4624 logs\eventlog.txt`.

successMessage: TargetUserName: Student. The laptop goes back to that account's owner, and the form is complete. Finding the one line that answers the question is the whole job.
